q-36521:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

Hence, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x} & =\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂y∂{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((x{y}^{2}+2y){e}^{xy}+2{z}^{3}) \\  & =(x{y}^{2}+2y)\cdot x{e}^{xy}+(2xy+2)\cdot {e}^{xy}+0 \\  & =({x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4xy+2){e}^{xy}.\end{aligned}
$$

In addition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂z}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(6x{z}^{2}) \\  & =12xz.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate both partial derivatives at the point $(1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}{|}_{(1,0,1)} & =(0+0+2){e}^{0}=2 \\ \frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,0,1)} & =12(1)(1)=12\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}{|}_{(1,0,1)}+\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,0,1)} & =2+12=14.\end{aligned}
$$

q-65132:
As the function and its first, second, and third-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ we must have ${f}_{yxx}(x,y)={f}_{xxy}(x,y).$ 

Therefore, we can swap the order of the subscripts in the first term. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yxx}(0,3)+{f}_{xx}(0,3)-{f}_{xxy}(0,3) & ={f}_{yxx}(0,3)+{f}_{xx}(0,3)-{f}_{yxx}(0,3) \\  & =\cancel{{f}_{yxx}(0,3)}+{f}_{xx}(0,3)-\cancel{{f}_{yxx}(0,3)} \\  & ={f}_{xx}(0,3) \\  & =6-(3){e}^{0} \\  & =6-3 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

q-129446:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\sqrt{y}-y\sqrt{x}) \\  & =\sqrt{y}-\frac{y}{2\sqrt{x}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\sqrt{y}-y\sqrt{x}) \\  & =\frac{x}{2\sqrt{y}}-\sqrt{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y)=(1,4):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,4) & =\sqrt{4}-\frac{4}{2\sqrt{1}}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,4) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{4}}-\sqrt{1}=-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-(-2) & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,4)+(y-4)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,4) \\ z+2 & =0(x-1)-\frac{3}{4}(y-4) \\ z+2 & =-\frac{3}{4}y+3 \\ \frac{3}{4}y+z-1 & =0 \\ 3y+4z-4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

q-129444:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-x{y}^{2}) \\  & =-{y}^{2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y-x{y}^{2}) \\  & =1-2xy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y)=(-1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(-1,1) & =-{1}^{2}=-1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(-1,1) & =1-2(-1)(1)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-2 & =(x-(-1))\frac{∂f}{∂x}(-1,1)+(y-1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(-1,1) \\ z-2 & =-(x+1)+3(y-1) \\ z-2 & =-x+3y-4 \\ x-3y+z+2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

q-37604:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x}+{e}^{y}-{e}^{z})={e}^{x} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x}+{e}^{y}-{e}^{z})={e}^{y} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{x}+{e}^{y}-{e}^{z})=-{e}^{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,1) & ={e}^{1}=e \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,1) & ={e}^{1}=e \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,1) & =-{e}^{1}=-e\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-e & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,1)+(y-1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,1) \\ w-e & =e(x-1)+e(y-1)-e(z-1) \\ w-e & =ex-e+ey-e-ez+e \\ -ex-ey+ez+w & =0 \\ ex+ey-ez-w & =0\end{aligned}
$$

q-129485:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz))=4\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz) \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz))=\frac{4xz}{1+{y}^{2}{z}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz))=\frac{4xy}{1+{y}^{2}{z}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(-1,1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(-1,1,1) & =4\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1\cdot 1)=\pi  \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(-1,1,1) & =\frac{4(-1)(1)}{1+({1}^{2})({1}^{2})}=-2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(-1,1,1) & =\frac{4(-1)(1)}{1+({1}^{2})({1}^{2})}=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-(-\pi ) & =(x-(-1))\frac{∂f}{∂x}(-1,1,1)+(y-1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(-1,1,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(-1,1,1) \\ w+\pi  & =\pi (x+1)-2(y-1)-2(z-1) \\ w+\pi  & =\pi x-2y-2z+4+\pi  \\ \pi x-2y-2z-w+4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

q-73860:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}-3x+{y}^{2}+2y) \\  & =3{x}^{2}-3 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}-3x+{y}^{2}+2y) \\  & =2y+2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨3{x}^{2}-3,\,2y+2,\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-3=0 \\ 2y+2=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $x=\pm 1$ while the second equation gives $y=-1.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=-1$ and $y=-1$ into our function, we get

$$
z=(-1)^{3}-3(-1)+(-1)^{2}+2(-1)=1.
$$

Substituting $x=1$ and $y=-1$ into our function, we get

$$
z=(1)^{3}-3(1)+(-1)^{2}+2(-1)=-3.
$$

Therefore, the points where the tangent plane is horizontal are $(-1,-1,1)$ and $(1,-1,-3).$

q-37982:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3xy-\operatorname{ln}⁡y) \\  & =3y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3xy-\operatorname{ln}⁡y) \\  & =3x-\frac{1}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨3y,\,3x-\frac{1}{y},\,-1⟩
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨3,5,-1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨3y,\,3x-\frac{1}{y},\,-1⟩=⟨3,5,-1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}3cy=3 \\ 3cx-\frac{c}{y}=5 \\ -c=-1\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
3(1)y=3\,⟹\,y=1.
$$

And substituting $c=1$ and $y=1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
3(1)x-\frac{1}{1}=5\,⟹\,x=2.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=2$ and $y=1$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =3xy-\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\  & =3(2)(1)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector  $v$ at $(2,1,6).$

q-98328:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,-2)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,-2)+∇f(-1,-2)\cdot ⟨x+1,y+2⟩ \\  & =f(-1,-2)+⟨{f}_{x}(-1,-2),{f}_{y}(-1,-2)⟩\cdot ⟨x+1,y+2⟩ \\  & =4+⟨4,-2⟩\cdot ⟨x+1,y+2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(-1.05,-1.96)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=-1.05$ and $y=-1.96,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-1.05,-1.96) & ≈4+⟨4,-2⟩\cdot ⟨-1.05+1,-1.96+2⟩ \\  & =4+⟨4,-2⟩\cdot ⟨-0.05,0.04⟩ \\  & =4-0.20-0.08 \\  & =3.72\end{aligned}
$$

q-129631:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,0)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(2,0)+∇f(2,0)\cdot ⟨x-2,y-0⟩ \\  & =f(2,0)+⟨{f}_{x}(2,0),{f}_{y}(2,0)⟩\cdot ⟨x-2,y⟩ \\  & =0+⟨0,2⟩\cdot ⟨x-2,y⟩ \\  & =⟨0,2⟩\cdot ⟨x-2,y⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(2.01,0.02)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=2.01$ and $y=0.02,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2.01,0.02) & ≈⟨0,2⟩\cdot ⟨2.01-2,0.02⟩ \\  & =⟨0,2⟩\cdot ⟨0.01,0.02⟩ \\  & =0(0.01)+2(0.02) \\  & =0+0.04 \\  & =0.04\end{aligned}
$$

q-98340:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,-1,2)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,-1,2)+∇f(1,-1,2)\cdot ⟨x-1,y+1,z-2⟩ \\  & =f(1,-1,2)+⟨{f}_{x}(1,-1,2),{f}_{y}(1,-1,2),{f}_{z}(1,-1,2)⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y+1,z-2⟩ \\  & =6+⟨-4,-1,3⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y+1,z-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(1.04,-0.99,2.02)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=1.04,$ $y=-0.99,$ and $z=2.02$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1.04,-0.99,2.02) & ≈6+⟨-4,-1,3⟩\cdot ⟨1.04-1,-0.99+1,2.02-2⟩ \\  & =6+⟨-4,-1,3⟩\cdot ⟨0.04,0.01,0.02⟩ \\  & =6-0.16-0.01+0.06 \\  & =5.89\end{aligned}
$$

q-129659:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(3,2,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(3,2,1)+∇f(3,2,1)\cdot ⟨x-3,y-2,z-1⟩ \\  & =12+⟨{f}_{x}(3,2,1),{f}_{y}(3,2,1),{f}_{z}(3,2,1)⟩\cdot ⟨x-3,y-2,z-1⟩ \\  & =12+⟨4,12,36⟩\cdot ⟨x-3,y-2,z-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(2.97,2.1,1.04)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=2.97,$ $y=2.1,$ and $z=1.04$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2.97,2.1,1.04) & ≈12+⟨4,12,36⟩\cdot ⟨2.97-3,2.1-2,1.04-1⟩ \\  & =12+⟨4,12,36⟩\cdot ⟨-0.03,0.1,0.04⟩ \\  & =12+4(-0.03)+12(0.1)+36(0.04) \\  & =12-0.12+1.2+1.44 \\  & =14.52\end{aligned}
$$

q-129748:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,-1,-1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,-1,-1)+∇f(1,-1,-1)\cdot ⟨x-1,y+1,z+1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(1,-1,-1)=1.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =yz\,⇒\,{f}_{x}(1,-1,-1)=1, \\ {f}_{y} & =xz\,⇒\,{f}_{y}(1,-1,-1)=-1, \\ {f}_{z} & =xy\,⇒\,{f}_{z}(1,-1,-1)=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(1,-1,-1)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(1,-1,-1) & =⟨{f}_{x}(1,-1,-1),{f}_{y}(1,-1,-1),{f}_{z}(1,-1,-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,-1,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,-1,-1)+∇f(1,-1,-1)\cdot ⟨x-1,y+1,z+1⟩ \\  & ≈1+⟨1,-1,-1⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y+1,z+1⟩ \\  & ≈1+(x-1)-(y+1)-(z+1) \\  & ≈-2+x-y-z.\end{aligned}
$$

q-98554:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,1,e)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,1,e)+∇f(1,1,e)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1,z-e⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(1,1,e)=0.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =y\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{x}(1,1,e)=1, \\ {f}_{y} & =x\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{y}(1,1,e)=1, \\ {f}_{z} & =-\frac{1}{z}\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{z}(1,1,e)=-\frac{1}{e}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(1,1,e)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(1,1,e) & =⟨1,1,-\frac{1}{e}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,1,e)+∇f(1,1,e)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1,z-e⟩ \\  & =0+⟨1,1,-\frac{1}{e}⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1,z-e⟩ \\  & =0+1(x-1)+1(y-1)-\frac{1}{e}(z-e) \\  & =-1+x+y-\frac{z}{e}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-160406:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x={e}^{u+v}$ and $y={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{u+v} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & ={e}^{u+v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =2v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{u+v} & {e}^{u+v} \\ \,\text{ }2u\, & \,\text{ }2v\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{u+v}\cdot 2v-{e}^{u+v}\cdot 2u \\  & =2{e}^{u+v}(v-u).\end{aligned}
$$

q-81264:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Here, we have $x(u,v)={u}^{2}-{v}^{2}$ and $y(u,v)={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}.$  

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-2v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =2v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2u & -2v \\ 2u & 2v\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u\cdot 2v-(-2v)\cdot 2u \\  & =4uv+4uv \\  & =8uv.\end{aligned}
$$
